summary.text: A warm front is the leading edge of a warm air mass that is replacing a cooler air mass.
Being lighter, the warm air cannot push the cold air aside, so it slides slowly up over it, cools, and forms widespread cloud.
Warm fronts move more slowly than cold fronts, and rain usually increases as one nears, followed by clearing and warming once it passes.

items.prompt: High wispy clouds keep spreading across the sky and your barometer starts to fall. Roughly how soon is rain likely?
items.explain: When high clouds steadily invade the sky and pressure begins to fall, precipitation is likely about 6 to 8 hours away.

items.prompt: At a warm front, why does the warm air glide up over the cold air instead of shoving it away?

options.label: The warm air is less dense and lighter
The cold air is moving faster
The warm air holds no moisture

items.explain: Warm air is less dense, so it cannot displace the cooler air and is forced upward over it in a process called overrunning.

items.prompt: A warm front has just moved past your town. What usually happens to the weather soon after?
items.explain: Clearing and warming is usually rapid after a warm front passes.

items.prompt: A warm front with stable air is just arriving. What can they turn into at ground level?
items.explain: With a stable air mass, the clouds can reach all the way to the ground as fog when the front arrives.

items.prompt: The air arriving behind a warm front was warmed over the ocean. How does it compare with the air ahead of it?
items.explain: If the warmer air comes from over the ocean, it is not only warmer but also moister than the air ahead.

items.prompt: A warm front is approaching on a calm, stable day. What kind of cloud mostly fills the sky ahead of it?

options.label: No cloud, just clear blue sky

items.explain: Clouds ahead of a warm front are mostly stratiform, meaning flat and layered.

paragraphs.heading: What a warm front is
paragraphs.text: A warm front is the leading edge of a warm air mass that is taking the place of cooler air. An air mass is a large body of air with similar temperature and humidity throughout, which forms over a source region. Across a warm front the density of the air changes sharply, and the front usually sits on the side of a temperature contrast that faces the equator.

paragraphs.heading: Riding up over cold air
paragraphs.text: Warm air is lighter than cold air, so the two are unlikely to mix. Instead of pushing the cooler air out of the way, the warm air is forced to slide up over it, a process called overrunning. The boundary slopes gently, about 1:200, so the lifting is slow but steady. As the warm air climbs into lower pressure it expands and cools, and its water vapor condenses into wide sheets of cloud.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the sky
paragraphs.text: The first sign of an approaching warm front is usually high cirrus cloud, which turns into cirrostratus as the front gets nearer. If those high clouds keep spreading and the barometer starts to drop, precipitation is likely about 6 to 8 hours away. When the clouds thicken and lower into altostratus or altocumulus, the front is closer and precipitation may start in under six hours. Once the clouds have thickened down to 2,500 metres (8,200 ft) above the ground, heavy nimbostratus can begin to release it, with low stratus and stratocumulus forming underneath.

paragraphs.heading: A slow mover
paragraphs.text: Warm fronts lie in wider troughs of low pressure than cold fronts and travel more slowly than the cold fronts that usually follow them. That is because cold air is denser and harder to shift off the ground, which also spreads the temperature change over a wider area. Warm fronts generally move from southwest to northeast. The clouds ahead of one are mostly layered, stratiform clouds, rain tends to build as it nears, and fog can form before it arrives.

paragraphs.heading: Stable or unstable air
paragraphs.text: After the front goes by, the sky usually clears and the air warms quickly. If the warm air came from over the ocean, it is moister as well as warmer than the air ahead. In stable air, rain keeps increasing until the front arrives, and clouds can reach right down to the ground as fog. In unstable air, thunderstorms can be tucked among the layered clouds ahead of the front and carry on after it, and the temperature change is larger.

paragraphs.heading: The warm sector and the map
paragraphs.text: Between the warm front and the cold front lies the warm sector, a mass of air near the ground on the equator side of an extratropical cyclone. Being warm and humid, this air can easily become unstable and feed thunderstorms, especially when the advancing cold front lifts it. On weather maps a warm front is drawn as a red line of semicircles pointing the way it travels, or as a solid red line on colored maps.
